issues.description: The entire Results section and all reported findings are based on randomly generated dummy data from Qualtrics, not actual participant responses. Despite repeated warnings in brackets, the abstract draws substantive conclusions ('found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning' and 'Results have supported the hypothesis'), presenting random noise as if it constitutes evidence for or against hypotheses. Any conclusion drawn from random data is scientifically meaningless.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.description: The Procedures section states that participants 'selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.' If participants self-select into conditions rather than being randomly assigned, the study is no longer an experiment but a quasi-experiment at best. Self-selection introduces systematic confounds that completely undermine any causal inference about the effects of identifiability or intervention on donation behavior. This is a fundamental departure from the original study which used random assignment.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The Design section describes the study as a 'single within-subject design,' but the original Studies 1 and 3 were between-subjects designs where each participant was assigned to one condition. The tables show different sample sizes per cell (e.g., 159, 175, 166), which is consistent with between-subjects, not within-subjects. If this is truly within-subjects, the statistical analyses (independent-groups ANOVA) would be inappropriate. If it is between-subjects, the description is incorrect.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.description: The original study gave participants $5 in real money and measured actual donation behavior (real monetary donation to Save the Children). The replication uses imaginary/hypothetical donations ('indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5'). This is a major construct validity concern, as hypothetical donations are known to systematically differ from real donations. This substantially weakens the replication's ability to test the same psychological phenomenon.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: Merging two separate studies into one
issues.description: The original Studies 1 and 3 were separate experiments with different designs (Study 1: 2×2; Study 3: one-way with 3 levels). Merging them into a single 2×3 design fundamentally changes the experimental structure, makes direct comparison to original effects problematic, and conflates explicit and implicit debiasing manipulations that were intentionally separated by the original authors. The claim of a 'close to very close replication' is questionable given this structural change.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect

issues.description: The randomly generated data shows an age range of 18–120 years with a mean of 67.80 (SD = 30.10) and median of 68. An age of 120 is biologically implausible, and such a high mean age is uncharacteristic of any realistic sample. While the authors note this is dummy data, presenting demographic tables with such values without flagging them as clearly impossible suggests lack of quality control in the simulated data, and that the analysis pipeline was not properly validated.
issues.quote: Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males

issues.description: The Results section interprets the random data substantively, including post-hoc comparisons and effect size discussions. For example, the authors report 'participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)' — a finding in the opposite direction of the identifiable victim effect — and interpret it as if it reflects a real pattern. No results from random data should be interpreted.
issues.quote: meaning that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: Abstract draws conclusions from dummy data
issues.description: The abstract states that 'Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.' This conclusion is drawn entirely from randomly generated data and is scientifically invalid. The abstract should not present any substantive findings until real data are collected.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: The original study compensated participants with $5 (which also served as the donation amount). The replication lists compensation as 'Not specified.' Without real monetary stakes, the ecological validity of the donation task is severely compromised, and this represents an important deviation from the original procedure.
issues.quote: Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified

issues.description: The manuscript has no Discussion section. Even for a pre-registration document, there should be planned interpretive criteria or at minimum a placeholder for discussion. The absence means there is no theoretical interpretation, no consideration of limitations, and no framework for how results (once actual data are collected) should be interpreted.

issues.subcategory: Power analysis details absent from manuscript
issues.description: The sample size justification and power analysis are repeatedly deferred to supplementary materials rather than reported in the manuscript. The manuscript states 'The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary' but never specifies the target power, the effect size used for the power analysis, or the resulting minimum sample size. This is critical information for evaluating the study's ability to detect the effects of interest.
issues.quote: The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary under the section of "Power analysis of the original study effect".

issues.description: The study tests six separate two-way ANOVAs on segregated feelings (Table 13), plus additional post-hoc tests, without family-wise error correction across the set of dependent variables. While Bonferroni corrections are applied for pairwise comparisons within each ANOVA, no correction is applied across the six separate ANOVAs on different feeling items, inflating the overall Type I error rate substantially.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on segregated affective reactions

issues.description: In interpreting Table 10 post-hoc tests, the text reports means of M=2.54 (statistical) and M=2.24 (identifiable), but Table 7 shows identifiable victim conditions have means of 2.58 (intervention) and 2.50 (no intervention), while statistical victim conditions have means of 2.46 and 2.01. The marginal means are not reported in Table 7, and the values cited in the text do not obviously correspond to any tabled values, making it unclear where these numbers come from.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)

issues.description: The original study was conducted in a laboratory setting (student center) with real face-to-face interaction and a physical donation envelope. The replication moves to an online platform (Amazon Mechanical Turk), which changes the social context, demand characteristics, experimenter presence, and engagement level. This switch may substantially affect donation behavior and emotional responses, undermining comparability with the original.
issues.quote: Online survey Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.description: The original Study 3 did not include any explicit intervention (learning about the identifiable victim effect) in the joint condition — the joint presentation was itself the implicit manipulation. The replication applies the explicit intervention to the joint condition, fundamentally altering the logic of the implicit debiasing test. This conflates explicit and implicit debiasing and makes it impossible to isolate the implicit effect as originally designed.
issues.quote: Intervention applied to the joint condition To combine study 1 and 3 into a single study, intervention will be applied to the joint condition to allow the comparison of explicit and implicit manipulation with fewer confounds.

issues.description: Table 4 ('Difference and similarities between the original study and replication') contains two identical columns both labeled as Qualtrics generated responses with identical values. It appears one column should represent planned actual data collection, but as presented, the table is redundant and confusing.
issues.quote: Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.subcategory: Typos and misspellings of author names
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly misspells 'Slovic' as 'Solvic' when referring to Slovic (2007). This occurs multiple times in the introduction and raises concerns about the care taken in manuscript preparation.
issues.quote: Solvic (2007) argued for the drawbacks of the phenomenon to raise awareness on our indifference of numerous death in genocide.

issues.subcategory: Extension hypothesis not actually supported by reported results
issues.description: Hypothesis 6 states that 'An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims.' However, the significant post-hoc result (Table 14) is between statistical and joint conditions, not between identifiable and statistical conditions. The abstract nonetheless claims the hypothesis was supported. The actual data (even though dummy) do not align with the stated hypothesis.
issues.quote: Significant differences were found between the statistical victim condition and the joint condition, t(994)=2.47, SE=0.11, p=.041.

issues.description: The manuscript does not mention institutional review board (IRB) or ethics committee approval for the study, which is a standard requirement for human subjects research.

Several links in the manuscript are placeholders (e.g., 'enter link here' for presentation and peer review folders), and some internal references appear garbled (e.g., 'supplementary' text appearing inline without proper hyperlink formatting). This hinders transparency and reproducibility.
issues.quote: Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here>

issues.description: The original study used ordered probit regression as one of its main analyses, but the replication explicitly states this will not be conducted. No justification is provided for omitting this analysis, which may capture ordinal structure in the donation variable that ANOVA does not handle well.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression | a. effect of identifiability on donation | This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.description: The original study recruited university students in Pennsylvania, while the replication plans to use Amazon Mechanical Turk workers. MTurk workers differ from student samples in age, income, motivation, and familiarity with charitable giving scenarios. This population difference may interact with the phenomenon being studied, particularly regarding real vs. hypothetical donation behavior.
issues.quote: MTurk workers as participants We will recruit participants on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study recruited participants sitting inside the school centre of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.description: The manuscript mentions excluding participants with prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect and those who failed attention checks, but provides no details on the attention check items, the criteria for determining 'prior knowledge,' or how many participants were excluded from the dummy dataset. For a pre-registration, these criteria should be precisely specified.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The replication reports extremely small effect sizes (e.g., ηp² = .007 for identifiability on donation) compared to the original (ηp² = .06). While the data are dummy, the analysis pipeline and sample size would yield very small effects from random data, and the fact that some reached significance (p = .028) with N = 1000 illustrates a concern about confusing statistical significance with practical significance that should be addressed in the planned analysis.

issues.subcategory: Measurement of feelings in joint condition
issues.description: The original study did not measure affective feelings in the joint condition of Study 3, but the replication adds these measurements. While this could be informative, it changes the comparison structure and makes direct comparison of feeling results to the original study more complex. This deviation is acknowledged but its implications are not discussed.
issues.quote: Feelings variables measurement We will measure affective feelings in the Joint condition which was not measured in the original study.

issues.description: Table 3 refers to 'Hypothese 3 and 4' in the text preceding it, which is a grammatical error, but more importantly, Hypotheses 5a and 5b are combined in a single row making them difficult to distinguish. The hypothesis for the extension (H6) is also not clearly differentiated from the replication hypotheses in terms of confirmatory vs. exploratory status.
issues.quote: we modify the original hypotheses for the interaction effect of explicit or implicit intervention on the donation tendency of different victim groups, regarded as Hypothese 3 and 4.

issues.subcategory: Classification as 'close to very close' replication is debatable
issues.description: Given the numerous deviations — merging two studies, changing from real to hypothetical donation, moving from lab to online, changing population, adding intervention to the joint condition, and modifying DV stimuli — the classification as a 'close to very close replication' appears overly generous. Several of these changes (particularly hypothetical donation and self-selection into conditions) fundamentally alter the study's construct validity.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.subcategory: Correlation analysis without controlling for shared variance
issues.description: The correlation between aggregated feelings and donation is examined separately for each of the six conditions without any omnibus test or regression controlling for condition membership. With six separate correlations, there is inflated Type I error risk, and condition-specific sample sizes (N ≈ 159-175) may be underpowered for detecting small-to-moderate correlations.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.description: While a pre-registration link is provided, the manuscript does not state when the pre-registration was time-stamped relative to data collection. The claim that 'data collection was completed before analyses' is important but should be verifiable with clear dates for pre-registration, data collection start, and data collection end.
issues.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period.
